title: the man in the well
hookLine: a man hangs in a well, Time waiting below, and still reaches for a drop of honey
carry: samsara: held by time, still reaching for honey
tomorrow: why does Krishna hand the blind king an iron statue?

lines: A MAN HANGS IN A WELL.
cards: A traveler is lost in a thick forest full of wild animals. Running from them, he falls into a well, but he doesn't hit the bottom. Creepers catch him, and he hangs there, upside down.
Below him waits a great serpent. Above him, at the well's mouth, stands a dark elephant. Rats are gnawing at the roots of the tree that holds the creepers.
And from a honeycomb in the branches, a drop of honey falls toward his mouth. This is how Stri, the book of the women, begins: with Vidura telling a story to a grieving king.

teach.b: The war is over. In Hastinapura, the old blind king Dhritarashtra hears that Duryodhana and his brothers are dead, and he falls to the ground in grief.
His half-brother Vidura sits with him and tells a story: the man in the well. And what does the man do, hanging between the serpent and the elephant, with the rats chewing the roots?
He drinks the honey, and he wants more. Then Vidura explains. The forest is the world we wander in.
The well is the body. The serpent at the bottom is Time, which takes everything. The elephant is the year; the rats are the days and nights; the creepers are the hope of life that holds us.
The honey is the pleasures we keep reaching for, even here. Hindus have a name for this whole picture: samsara, the turning world of birth and death, where Time carries off everything that's born.
Vidura is describing everyone, the king included.

teach.h: FOR THE BORN, DEATH IS CERTAIN
teach.b: It's the same truth Krishna gives Arjuna in the Gita: for whoever is born, death is certain, so don't grieve as if it shouldn't have happened. That's why, at a death, you may hear a Hindu family say quietly, it's samsara.
It doesn't mean don't be sad. It means this comes to all of us, and nobody is alone in the well.

how: Vidura's parable of the man in the well is retold by Hindu teachers as a picture of samsara, and many Hindus chant the Mahamrityunjaya mantra for the sick and the dying.

games.q: the man in the well — tap the pairs.

s: the man in the well gave up wanting anything
he drank the honey and wanted more, still wishing to live.
Vidura told the parable to comfort Dhritarashtra
he told it to the grieving king after the news of his sons.
saying 'it's samsara' at a death means grief is wrong
Vidura said it sitting beside a grieving king: death comes to all, and no one is alone in the well.

games.q: you're the man hanging in the well. a serpent waits below, rats gnaw the roots, and a drop of honey falls toward your mouth. what do you do?
o: climb the creepers toward the elephant.
drink the honey and wish for more.
let go and drop to the bottom.
games.why: he drinks the honey and wants more. Vidura says that's samsara: every one of us, held by Time, still reaching.

practice: Many Hindus chant the Mahamrityunjaya mantra for the sick and the dying. It asks Shiva for freedom from death's grip, the way a ripe cucumber slips easily from its vine.

Sit quietly and picture the man's creepers, then that ripe fruit letting go without a struggle. Breathe in, holding on; breathe out, loosening. If you pray, you can say the mantra, or simply ask to let go well when it's time.
If you don't, rest with the picture of the ripe fruit.
